newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz gets chance at anti-Islamist pact.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz gets chance at anti-Islamist pact.

text.p: Turkey's president on Friday handed secularist Mesut Yilmaz the difficult task of forging a new coalition in a bid to end months of turmoil over the role of Islam in public life.
"A while ago, the president gave me the responsibility to form a new government," Yilmaz told reporters at the presidential palace.
Yilmaz, 50, will now have to patch together a coalition from among a host of squabbling secularist leaders after this week's resignation of Necmettin Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader.

Despite apparently stiff odds -- his Motherland Party fields just 129 MPs in the 550-seat parliament -- Yilmaz said he was confident he could hammer together a cabinet list by June 30 to lead the country to early polls next spring.
"In nine days, that is the second Monday from now, I will give the government list to the president," he said. He was not expected to invite the Islamists into a new coalition.
Erbakan quit on Wednesday after rumblings from the army that it was prepared to use to force against his Islamist supporters.
"The president gave Yilmaz the responsiblity to form a government that will defuse the current tension in the country," Demirel's office said in a statement.

Two leftist parties have said they were prepared to back Yilmaz in an "Islamist-free" coalition, but Yilmaz would still require substantial defections from a rival conservative party, led by his personal rival Tansu Ciller.
Yilmaz, a staid conservative, said he would meet the leaders of the other secularist parties including Ciller, next Tuesday.
Pro-Western Ciller, who served as Erbakan's deputy prime minister, was also in the running for the top job. She has the backing of 282 deputies, at least on paper.

But Ciller, who became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993, is distrusted by the secularist establishment for going into coalition with the Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party last year after pledging not to do so.
Aides to Yilmaz were up-beat.

"Hope for a new start for the country has been born," party spokesman Cumhur Ersumer told a news conference before the formal announcement. "(The Motherland Party) is ready to take over the duties of the administration."
The Istanbul stock market index, battered by recent political chaos, ended up 2.56 percent on hopes Yilmaz would get the nod from Demirel. Trading closed before the announcement.
Erbakan had asked Demirel to approve a plan under which Ciller would head a new coalition with the Islamists to take Turkey to early elections.
But Demirel, a veteran of political in-fighting, relied on Turkish tradition and turned to Yilmaz as leader of the second-biggest faction in parliament after Erbakan himself.

Yilmaz, prime minister twice since 1991, went to Ankara's main Kocatepe mosque for Friday prayers after Demirel's invitation. A bouquet of flowers sent by a well-wisher stood outside the Yilmaz family home, witnesses said.
Anatolian news agency said armed forces chief General Ismail Hakki Karadayi arrived at Demirel's residence an hour after the Yilmaz appointment for talks with the president.
The army has a long history of intervention in politics, deposing three governments in the last four decades before playing a key role in forcing Erbakan out.

Top commanders have branded religious activism as "public enemy number one" for NATO member Turkey. The generals had become increasingly critical in recent weeks of Erbakan's attempts to water down Turkey's strict secularism.
